The gas clings to the trench like a greasy, yellow-green fog, pooling in the shell-holes where the air is still. The soldier—let’s call him Brennan—doesn’t see it coming; he smells it first, a sharp, chlorinated stench like bleach poured over rotting hay, and then his throat begins to seize.

**The Body Betrays Him**

His lungs, once the bellows of a healthy twenty-year-old, become a battlefield. The alveoli—those delicate air sacs—begin to weep fluid. He coughs, a wet, rattling sound, and a pink-tinged froth bubbles at the corners of his mouth, each bubble a tiny, bursting coffin of oxygen-starved tissue. His chest heaves, but the breath won’t come; the diaphragm spasms against a wall of liquid building in his bronchial tubes. He is drowning, but the water is inside him, rising with every panicked gulp.

His lips turn the color of bruised plums—cyanosis creeping in from the extremities as his blood fails to carry oxygen. His fingernails, pressed against the muddy trench wall for support, pale to a waxy blue. The gas has burned the moist membranes of his eyes; tears stream down his face, mixing with the mucus, stinging chemical burns that feel like ground glass embedded in his eyelids. His skin, where the gas has touched exposed wrists and neck, prickles with a thousand needle-stings, blistering into angry, weeping welts if it’s mustard; if it’s phosgene, the damage is invisible and insidious, a delayed suffocation that tightens like a noose hours later.

He claws at his throat, nails scoring red lines into his neck, trying to claw out the fluid filling his lungs. Each inhalation is a battle: a wet, gurgling rasp, as though he’s sucking air through a straw clogged with wet concrete. His ribs crack against the pressure as he tries to expand them, but the chest feels locked in a vise of fluid and inflammation.

**The Mind Unravels**

Mentally, he is unmoored. The terror is pre-verbal, a lizard-brain scream that bypasses language. He knows, with a horrible, crystalline clarity, that he is dying not by bullet or blade, but by the very air he must breathe to live. The trench around him dissolves into a nightmare of green haze. His comrades’ faces—if he can see them through the streaming, burning eyes—are distorted, monstrous, or perhaps they are already dead and he is alone.

There is a profound, existential loneliness in chemical warfare. He cannot scream for help; the attempt produces only a bubbling, gurgling croak. He is conscious of his own body shutting down, a spectator to his own asphyxiation. Panic gives way to a terrible, resigned clarity: *This is how I end. Not with glory. With fluid in my lungs and foam on my lips.*

His thoughts fragment. He thinks of his mother’s kitchen. He thinks of the drill sergeant’s voice. He thinks of the sweet, impossible relief of a deep, clean breath—a memory now as distant as childhood. The gas has stripped away dignity; he is reduced to a gasping, twitching thing, clawing at the earth, leaving smears of bloody froth on the duckboards.

Time dilates. A minute is an eternity of suffocation. He wants to run, but his legs are lead; the effort of movement steals the precious, dwindling oxygen from his starved brain. Confusion sets in—he doesn’t know if he’s standing or lying down. The world narrows to the single, desperate act of trying to pull air into lungs that have become waterlogged sponges.

He dies, if he dies, conscious, aware, fighting for each microgram of oxygen, a human bellows failing against the chemistry of war.

The rain against the window was the only sound for a long moment. Vincent Corleone didn’t look up from his ledger, his fountain pen scratching a steady, metronomic rhythm across the page.

Across the desk, Marco sat with his hands folded, his suit immaculate, his face carefully blank.

“Rossi,” Vincent said, not pausing in his accounting. “How long has he been with the family?”

“Fifteen years, Vince. Since the Brooklyn days.”

Vincent finally capped the pen. He reached for the tumbler of scotch, poured two fingers, and slid the glass across the mahogany without looking. “And how long has he been... *uncooperative*?”

Marco didn’t flinch. “Since Tuesday. The feds picked him up, but he’s singing. He’s giving them names. He’s giving them routes.”

The pen tapped once against the blotter. A finality to it.

“That’s unfortunate,” Vincent said. His voice was soft, almost gentle, the way a man might discuss the weather. “Rossi was always such a... dedicated employee. It’s a shame when talent goes to waste, isn’t it?”

He stood, walked to the window, and stared out at the gray Manhattan dusk. “I think,” he continued, “it’s time we considered his retirement package. Permanent, of course. Full benefits. No more late nights, no more stress. Just... eternal rest.”

Marco nodded slowly. “He has a wife. Two kids.”

“Then we’ll make sure they’re... taken care of. Generous severance. A nice house in the country. Somewhere quiet.” Vincent turned, and for the first time, his eyes met Marco’s—cold, flat, ancient. “I want him to go to sleep tonight, Marco. And I don’t want him to wake up. Do you understand?”

“Perfectly, Vince.”

Vincent smiled, a thin, bloodless thing. “Good. Then let’s arrange the transition. Make it clean. Make it look like... an accident. A man who simply stepped off the edge of the world and kept falling. No pain. No suffering. Just... silence.”

He returned to his chair, picked up his pen. “And Marco? Tell the family. Tell them Rossi has been promoted. Promoted to a position where he can never betray us again.”

Outside, the rain began to fall harder.

The impact comes first—a thunderclap of sod, then the percussion of clods striking pine. A handful of loam sifts through the seams, dusting the charcoal wool of the suit, the polished shoes. Then silence, heavy and absolute, until the second shovelful lands.

**The weight.**

It is not immediate. At first, it is merely sound—the muffled *thump-thump-thump* of earth being packed, a heartbeat from above that is not a heartbeat at all. But then the lid begins to complain. A groan, like the hull of a ship in a storm, as six feet of compressed soil settles into the grain. The pressure builds incrementally, each additional shovel adding pounds, then tons. The wood flexes inward, bowing like a held breath. The air inside the box compresses, becoming thick, metallic, tasting of rust and grave-mold. Every inhalation requires effort now; every exhalation fogs the darkness with condensation that drips onto the face like cold sweat.

**The dark.**

There is no light. Not a pinprick, not a suggestion of a glow. The darkness is a physical presence, pressing against the eyeballs, filling the mouth, seeping into the ears. The space is exact—six feet long, two wide, eighteen inches high. Shoulders brush the varnished sides. Knees press against the footboard. The coffin is a second skin, then a vice. The silence is so complete it has texture; it hums in the molars, a low-frequency drone that vibrates in the sternum. Time unravels. A minute stretches into an hour; an hour becomes an eternity of waiting for the next shovel.

**The clawing.**

The hands move before the mind catches up. Fingers splay against the lid, nails finding the seams, the brass handles, the varnish. They scrape—a sound like a mouse trapped in a wall, frantic and rhythmic. *Scritch. Scritch. Scritch.* The wood is smooth, slick with moisture from the earth above, offering no purchase. Nails split against the grain, tearing back, leaving crescent-moon wounds that weep blood onto the silk lining. The palms press flat against the ceiling of the box, pushing upward, muscles trembling with the effort of lifting something that weighs as much as a car, then a truck, then a mountain. The knuckles whiten. The fingertips go numb, then burn, then go numb again.

Above, the dirt continues to fall. It is relentless, patient, geological. Each layer adds to the suffocation, pressing the lid down, down, until the coffin creaks and the air inside grows thinner, until the clawing slows, becomes a twitch, becomes stillness—as the weight above becomes absolute, and the dark becomes total.

The gaslight flickered against the damask wallpaper, casting long shadows across the drawing room as the clock struck four. Mrs. Ashford watched her husband’s hand tremble around the porcelain cup—china so thin it sang when tapped, now cradled between fingers that had grown papery with age.

He drank.

The first sign was the spasm in his throat. Not a cough, but a convulsion—a sudden, violent arching of the spine that sent the saucer clattering against the marble mantelpiece. His eyes, pale blue and rheumy with cataracts, bulged wide as saucers. The corners of his mouth drew back from his teeth in a rictus that was not quite a grimace, revealing gums that had gone the color of old bruises.

Then the color left him.

It drained from his face in visible waves, starting at the temples and racing downward like ink spreading through water. His skin took on a translucent, waxy quality, the blue veins beneath standing out in stark relief. A thin line of saliva—tinged with rust—appeared at the corner of his mouth. He clawed at his collar, fingers scrabbling at the starched linen, nails whitening as if trying to tear the air itself.

"Henry?" Mrs. Ashford’s voice remained steady, crystalline. She did not move to help.

The convulsions began in earnest. His body became a battleground of contradictory forces—the back arching so severely his heels nearly touched the back of his head, then collapsing forward until his forehead struck the mahogany table with a wet, cracking sound. His limbs jerked in violent, arrhythmic spasms, knocking over the sugar tongs, sending a spoon skittering across the Axminster carpet. Foam appeared at his lips, pink and frothy, bubbling with each ragged exhalation.

His breathing changed. It became a wet, rattling sound—like a bellows drawing through water. The pupils dilated, consuming the irises until his eyes were pools of black glass. A single drop of blood, dark as port wine, seeped from his nostril, tracing a crimson path down his upper lip.

Mrs. Ashford rose from her settee, the rustle of her bombazine skirt loud in the sudden stillness. She approached the chair where her husband now slumped, his head lolling to one side, jaw slack. His chest rose and fell in shallow, desperate hiccups. The skin of his hands, visible where his gloves had slipped, had mottled into a purple lattice—livor mortis beginning its work even as the heart hammered against the ribs in a futile, arrhythmic staccato.

He made a sound then—a high, keening whine that seemed to come from deep in his chest, vibrating through the sternum. His fingers, blue at the tips, twitched against the upholstery. One last convulsion seized him, rigid as a board, teeth clicking together like castanets, before the body went slack.

The tea cup lay on its side beside him, the remaining liquid darkening the Persian rug like a spreading bruise.

Mrs. Ashford adjusted her spectacles and rang for the maid. Outside, the November fog pressed against the windows, gray and patient.

The Harvest Pit smelled of ozone, rust, and the copper-sweet tang of old blood baked into concrete. Above the circular arena, holographic advertisements flickered in a loop—*Nutrient Paste: 90% Daily Value. Compliance is Nourishment.*—casting a sickly green glow over the two figures standing at opposite ends of the stained floor.

They did not wear names. They wore numbers stenciled in black paint on their chests: 47 and 112.

47 was gaunt, ribs pressing against skin like xylophone keys. He had not eaten in four days. His weapon was a length of rebar, sharpened on one end, wrapped in scavenged fabric at the grip. 112 was younger, broader, still carrying the last of yesterday's allocation in her muscles, armed with a hooked meat cleaver that had been sterilized until it gleamed. Both wore the grey tunic of the Unassigned, their ankles chained to the floor by retractable carbon-fiber tethers that allowed a twenty-foot radius of movement before snapping taut.

The crowd—three thousand spectators in the upper tiers, their faces obscured by breathing masks—did not cheer when the gates opened. They *hungered*. The sound was a low, grinding moan, the collective inhale of a starving beast.

The tether released.

47 moved first, but 112 was faster. The cleaver caught him across the shoulder, tearing fabric and skin. 47 stumbled, felt warmth spreading down his left side, and lunged. They grappled at the center of the pit, a tangle of elbows and knees, breath ragged and wet. 47’s fingers found 112’s throat, squeezing. She gurgled, her cleaver scraping uselessly against his ribs, and drove her knee upward into his gut. He doubled over, exposing his back.

112 raised the cleaver for a downward strike to the spine—

47 twisted, catching her wrist. He had been saving this. With a roar that tore his vocal cords, he drove the sharpened rebar upward, not into her chest, but beneath her jaw, angling toward the base of her skull. The steel punched through cartilage and sinew with a wet, sickening *thunk*. 112’s eyes widened, went blank. Her cleaver clattered against the concrete. Her hands spasmed once, twice, then went limp against 47’s chest.

47 did not let go. He held the rebar buried to the hilt, his forehead pressed against 112’s, watching the light drain from her eyes. Blood bubbled from her lips, hot and pink, splattering against his number. He felt her heartbeat flutter against his palm—a trapped bird—then still.

Silence fell over the Pit, broken only by the drip of blood and the hum of the ventilation system.

The overhead speakers crackled. *"Unit 112 terminated. Unit 47 victorious. Ration allocation: Seven days. Protein supplement: Granted."*

A panel in the arena floor hissed open, dispensing a sealed foil packet and a small vial of water. 47 released the rebar. 112’s body collapsed, her chain going slack with a heavy *clang*. He stood over her, swaying, the packet already clutched in his trembling hand, his chest heaving as he tried to remember what fullness felt like.

In the stands, the crowd exhaled, disappointed that the spectacle had ended so quickly, already turning their attention to the next pairing scheduled for the afternoon meal.

Each shot is a punctuation mark in the sentence of his survival—*crack-crack-crack*—three rounds chewing through the pursuing sedan’s windshield, spiderwebbing the glass, sending fragments glittering across three lanes of asphalt like deadly confetti.

Time dilates. His heart is a fist hammering against his sternum, a biological metronome set to *flight*. Adrenaline floods his synapses, sharpening the screech of tires into crystalline clarity, turning the smell of burning rubber and ozone into a perfume. The world narrows to the geometry of escape: the arc of his muzzle flash illuminating the cabin in strobe-like bursts, the spent brass casings dancing across the passenger seat like metallic tumbleweeds, the rearview mirror vibrating with the thunder of his own gunfire.

But the rush curdles with horror.

Through the side window, he sees them—the bystanders. A woman pushing a stroller freezes at the crosswalk, her eyes wide as saucers, the baby’s bottle forgotten. A cyclist swerves, his messenger bag catching the side of a taxi, sending him sprawling into the street. An elderly man drops his groceries as his sedan fishtains beneath the character’s bumper, cans of soup scattering across the pavement like shrapnel.

He fires again. The recoil kicks his shoulder, a reminder of Newton’s laws, of equal and opposite reaction. Behind him, the pursuers’ SUV lurches, fishtailing, its driver fighting for control as bullets chew through its bumper. But the danger has metastasized beyond the chase. A rickshaw taxi cuts too close; the driver’s scream is swallowed by the roar of engines. A shop window explodes outward as his vehicle clips a parked van, glass raining onto the sidewalk where a businessman dives behind a newspaper stand, his briefcase abandoned, papers fluttering like wounded birds.

His breath comes in ragged, hyperventilated gasps. The adrenaline is a burning wire threaded through his veins, making his fingers numb around the grip, making the muzzle flash feel like a heartbeat externalized. Every swerve is a calculus of survival, but the math is bloody: for every foot he gains on his pursuers, the margin of safety for the woman with the stroller shrinks. For every bullet he fires backward, the risk of a ricochet finding an innocent skull increases exponentially.

He grits his teeth, jaw aching, and fires again—not at the pursuers now, but into the air, a warning shot that echoes off the canyon of downtown buildings. The sound bounces between steel and glass, a sonic reminder that he is a storm moving through a city of glass. The wrench felt cold in Elias's palm, a familiar weight. He had done this before—not to cars, but to the idea of justice. Three years ago, Marcus Hale had walked out of that courtroom smiling, his lawyer shaking hands, his bank account intact after the embezzlement that had taken the clinic, the savings, the future. Now the sedan sat in the driveway, silver and gleaming, waiting to carry Marcus to another dinner, another deal, another life he hadn't earned.

Elias's fingers found the brake line. One cut. Clean. Invisible.

*He deserves to feel what I felt,* Elias told himself as the fluid beaded on the concrete, dark as old blood. *The terror. The helplessness. The moment when you realize the world has betrayed you and there's no appeal.*

He justified it through the ledger of his grief. Every sleepless night. Every anniversary of the empty chair. Every time he'd had to explain to his daughter why Grandma's house was gone, why the college fund was dust. Marcus had stolen not just money, but time—years he would never get back, moments of peace poisoned by the knowledge that the man who caused it breathed freely, ate well, slept soundly.

*It's not murder,* Elias whispered to the empty garage. *It's delayed justice. A correction. The universe balancing itself.*

He thought of the physics: the car would stop responding at the first curve, or maybe it wouldn't stop at all. Momentum and physics don't care about innocence. The mathematics of revenge was simple—one life for the ruin of dozens.

But as he wiped his hands on his jeans, the justification began to curdle. Elias saw Marcus not as a villain, but as a man with a daughter who loved him, a dog that waited by the door, a fear of heights that made him dizzy on balconies. The brake line was already cut. The damage was done. And in that silence, the weight of the wrench translated into something else: the understanding that two wrongs don't make a right, they just make a darker wrong.

He stood there until the streetlight flickered on outside, illuminating the cut cable glinting like a silver scar. The justification had been a story he told himself to survive the night, a way to turn unbearable pain into righteous action. But stories don't stop cars. Physics does. And physics doesn't forgive.

Elias walked away without calling the police, carrying the knowledge that he had become the thing he hated—not a man seeking justice, but a man manufacturing catastrophe. The revenge wasn't in the sabotage. The revenge was having to live with the knowledge that he had chosen to become a killer, and that the brakes would fail, and that someone would die, and that he would deserve every sleepless night that followed.

Outside, the silver sedan sat innocent and deadly, waiting for a morning that might never come.

After the last shell,
the silence has weight—
a stone dropped
into a well too deep
to echo.

They lie in the dust
like discarded clothes,
faces turned upward
to collect the clouds
that drift past
indifferent as gods.
No hand reaches
for a rifle.
No chest rises
to meet the morning.

The flies come first,
green and urgent,
conducting their small
religious services
over the open mouths,
the unblinking eyes.
They do not hurry,
nor do they weep.
They simply measure
the distance
between what was
and what will be
becoming.

Then the crows,
black commas
punctuating the flat
prose of the plain.
They walk with tilted heads,
judging the tenderness
of each throat,
the give of the flesh.
They are priests
of the necessary,
without sermon
or scripture,
only beaks
that know
the shape of ending.

Above, the buzzards turn
in slow orbits,
riding the heat
that rises from cooling bodies
like incense.
They have seen
this altar before—
Gettysburg, Verdun,
a thousand names
unspoken now.

The dead do not stir.
Their pockets hold
photographs and coins,
letters half-read,
all the small
evidence of lives
now reduced to stillness.
They have surrendered
even their fear.

Dusk settles
like a hand
over closed eyes.
The scavengers roost,
wings folded,
beaks tucked,
ants marching
in single file
across a forearm,
carrying the empire
of the living
piece by piece
into the dark.

The hunger had hollowed him out three days ago, leaving only a trembling husk that happened to walk on two legs. Now it sat in his gut like a living thing—gnawing, twisting, a knot of acid that made his vision swim with black spots. The scrap of protein he’d found, gray and suspicious, wrapped in foil that crinkled like dry leaves, was all that stood between him and the dark.

The dog didn’t bark. It didn’t need to. It simply *was*—a rangy silhouette of ribs and yellowed teeth, muscles coiled like springs beneath patchy fur the color of old rust. It had been watching him from the cracked asphalt since he’d unwrapped the meat, hackles raised, saliva dripping in silent metronomes onto the dust.

When it lunged, it was less an attack than a collision of desperation.

Jace didn’t think. Thinking required calories he didn’t have. He threw himself sideways, the foil tearing against his palm, and felt the dog’s jaws snap shut inches from his throat. The impact drove the air from his lungs. They crashed against the side of a rusted-out sedan, metal screaming, glass already gone, frame groaning. Jace’s shoulder hit first, then his hip, a shockwave of pain that paled beside the inferno in his stomach.

He swung his fist—not with strength, but with the wild, flailing desperation of a man drowning. His knuckles connected with the dog’s snout. Bone crunched. The animal yelped, a high, wet sound, but didn’t release its forward momentum. Jace felt the hot rush of its breath, rank and sour, against his face as they tumbled.

They rolled in the dust, a tangle of limbs and teeth. Jace clutched the meat to his chest with one arm, a pathetic shield, while his other hand clawed at the dog’s eyes, fingers digging into wet fur, seeking the soft globes beneath. The dog snarled, a guttural war that vibrated in Jace’s sternum, and snapped at his wrist. Teeth scraped bone. Jace screamed—not from pain, but from the violation of it, the animal claiming territory inside his skin.

He headbutted. His nose met the dog’s jaw with a sickening crack that echoed in his skull. For a moment, they were still, panting, two starving things locked in a tableau of mutual annihilation. The dog’s chest heaved, ribs working like bellows. Jace’s vision tunneled. He could taste copper—his own blood, or the dog’s, he couldn’t tell.

Then the hunger won.

Jace drove his knee upward, into the soft wedge beneath the dog’s ribs. The animal convulsed, a wet hiccup escaping its throat. Jace seized the moment, twisting, using every ounce of leverage his depleted body could muster. He heard something pop—cartilage, or tendon, or hope—and the dog’s jaws finally opened, releasing his wrist with a spray of red that splattered across the dust.

Jace scrambled backward, gasping, his hand a ruin of torn flesh and throbbing nerve endings. The dog lay panting, one eye swelling shut, whining now, pathetic and broken. Jace looked at it—really looked—and saw his own reflection: the same desperation, the same willingness to kill for a mouthful of sustenance.

His hands shook as he unwrapped the meat. It was warm now, tainted with his sweat and blood. He didn’t care. The fire had burned low to embers, painting the tent in shades of dying blood. Elias knelt over Thomas, whose shirt had been torn away to reveal a ragged black hole in his side, weeping dark arterial spray with each ragged breath. The whiskey bottle sat between them, half-empty, its glass slick with sweat and gun oil.

"Drink," Elias commanded, his voice cracking. He pressed the bottle to Thomas's lips. "All of it. It won't stop the pain, but it might stop you from screaming."

Thomas's teeth ground against the neck. He drank, coughing, tears tracking through the grime on his face. When he finished, his hand found Elias's wrist—not to pull away, but to grip with desperate strength. "Do it," he hissed through clenched teeth. "Before I bleed out on your boots."

Elias picked up the Bowie knife. It was his eating blade, the one his mother had given him. Now it would be a butcher's tool. He held it over the fire until the steel glowed cherry-red, then plunged it into the whiskey. The hiss of steam filled the silence. He wiped the blade on his pant leg, then doused it again. The smell of scorched hair mixed with the copper-sweet stench of Thomas's blood.

"Hold him," someone said from the shadows.

Marcus stepped forward, his big hands pressing down on Thomas's shoulders. Thomas arched, a sound tearing from his throat—not words, but pure animal agony as the cold steel kissed his skin.

Elias cut.

The blade parted flesh with a wet, obscene sound, like tearing heavy canvas. Thomas screamed, a high, broken thing that seemed to tear the canvas of the tent itself. Blood welled instantly, hot and thick, flooding Elias's fingers. He worked by touch alone, his vision swimming. The whiskey made Thomas's skin slippery; the knife skidded once, catching the edge of the wound, and Thomas's body went rigid, a board of pain.

"Fuck," Elias breathed. "Fuck, fuck, I'm sorry, Thomas, I'm so sorry—"

He found the bullet with his finger, probing the cavity. Thomas bucked so hard Marcus had to throw his weight across him, pinning him to the cot. Elias felt the lead sphere, jagged and hot, embedded near the rib. He pinched it with two fingers—felt the resistance, the sickening give of flesh as he pulled.

The bullet hit the tin plate with a *ping* that sounded like salvation.

Thomas went limp. Not unconscious—just emptied, his chest hitching in ragged, shallow draws.

"Got it," Elias whispered. His hands were shaking so badly he could barely thread the needle. He used dental floss from his kit, sterilized in more whiskey. Each stitch pulled the wound edges together, and each one drew a fresh gasp from Thomas. Elias sewed him shut like a split pelt, working with mechanical precision while his mind screamed at the horror of what he was doing.

When he finished, he poured the rest of the whiskey over the stitches. Thomas hissed, then laughed—a broken, delirious sound. "You magnificent bastard," he rasped. "You magnificent, horrible bastard."

Elias collapsed back on his heels, staring at his blood-soaked hands. The tent smelled of copper and shit and whiskey. Somewhere outside, wolves began to howl.

"He'll live," Elias said, his voice hollow. "If it doesn't get infected. If the fever doesn't take him."

Thomas gripped his hand, his fingers cold and clammy. "Then we make sure it doesn't."

Outside, the wind carried the scent of snow. Elias sat with his friend until dawn, listening to his breathing steady, watching the rise and fall of his chest, terrified that the next breath might be the last.

Glass became the first casualty. The bulletproof partition behind the vault door spiderwebbed under the pressure of automatic fire, cracks racing outward like frost on a winter pane. Then the front doors—thick, reinforced, supposedly impenetrable—exploded inward in a hurricane of crystalline shards. The air filled with a blizzard of diamond-dust, each shard catching the light from the strobing police cruisers outside, turning the lobby into a kaleidoscope of lethal confetti.

She was diving for the column when it hit.

The round came from somewhere—deflected off the floor, or sprayed wide from an officer's Glock, or maybe just the chaotic geometry of crossfire finding its mark. The impact was instantaneous and paradoxical: a searing, white-hot brand pressed against the bone, followed immediately by a strange, spreading numbness that made the arm feel detached, foreign.

She stumbled, the bag of money slipping from nerveless fingers, and hit the floor hard. The shoulder erupted in wet warmth. She tried to lift the arm—needed to, to run, to fight—but the muscles refused, locked in a spasm of shock. Above her, the glass continued to rain down, tinkling against the tile like a death knell, while the crossfire roared on, indifferent, hungry, turning the bank into a meat grinder of lead and shattered crystal.

The fluorescent light above the metal table hummed, casting a bruise-purple glow across the concrete floor. Elias sat in the chair, wrists secured with zip-ties that bit into his skin, his breath shallow and controlled—the only thing he had left to control.

Across from him, Mara didn't look at him. She was sharpening a scalpel on a whetstone, the *shink-shink* sound filling the silence like a metronome counting down to something inevitable.

"You know why we're here," she said, not looking up. Her voice was soft, almost conversational, the way she might discuss the weather.

Elias swallowed. His mouth was cotton. "I don't have anything to give you."

Mara set the scalpel down. The sound it made on the steel table was final, like a gavel. She leaned forward, elbows on her knees, and for the first time, her eyes met his. They were pale, almost colorless, and utterly devoid of mercy.

"That's not what I asked, Elias."

She stood, walked to the wall, and flipped a switch. A digital timer appeared on the concrete, glowing red: **00:04:59**.

"It works like this," she said, tapping the wall. "Every five minutes, the chair tilts back. Just a little. Two degrees. Not enough to hurt you yet. But your blood will start to rush to your head. You'll feel the pressure behind your eyes. The headache will start at the temples and work its way down your neck. By minute fifteen, you'll be begging for the lights to go out. By minute twenty, you'll be screaming. By minute twenty-five..." She paused, letting the implication hang. "Well. Let's just say you won't be conscious to give me anything anyway."

Elias felt his pulse hammering in his throat. The chair beneath him seemed to shift, though it hadn't moved—just his imagination, playing tricks, or perhaps the machine already starting its slow, imperceptible descent.

"I don't... I can't," he whispered.

"Can't or won't?" Mara moved closer, close enough that he could smell the antiseptic on her gloves. "There's a difference. One of them ends with you in a shallow grave. The other ends with you typing six characters into a keyboard and walking out of here with your dignity... mostly intact."

She reached out, her fingers hovering just above his cheek, not touching, but the threat of contact vibrating in the air between them.

"The password isn't for a bank account, Elias. It's for a server. A server that holds the location of three hundred people. Men, women, children who think you're their friend. Every minute you waste, I make a phone call. Every minute, someone disappears."

The timer beeped. **00:04:30**.

"The chair is already moving," Mara said, stepping back. "Feel it? That slight shift? In ninety seconds, your world gets a little heavier. In three minutes, it gets heavier still. And you have until the timer hits zero to decide if your loyalty to whatever cause is worth your optic nerves."

Elias stared at the numbers, watching them bleed red against the gray wall. He could hear his own heartbeat, a frantic drum against the silence. The room felt smaller, the air thinner.

"I..." His voice cracked. "It's not a word. It's... it's numbers."

"Then give me the numbers," Mara said, her voice dropping to a whisper. "Give me the numbers, Elias, before your own body becomes your enemy."

The timer flashed **00:03:00**.

"Three minutes," she said, and sat back down, picking up the scalpel again. The *shink-shink* of the blade on stone resumed, louder now, drowning out everything else.

Elias looked down at his hands, trembling in their restraints. The chair tilted, just a fraction, and he felt the first trickle of blood beginning its slow migration toward his skull.

"Please," he said, and the word tasted like ash.

The smoke came first—thick, black, and hungry, pouring under the door like a living thing. You coughed, but the cough only invited more poison down your throat. Your lungs burned, not with fire, but with a wet, drowning sensation, each inhale pulling razor shards of soot deeper into your chest. Your eyes streamed, blurring the world into a watercolor of orange and gray.

Then came the heat.

It pressed against your skin like a fever, raising angry red welts across your cheeks and forearms. You tried to pull your shirt over your face, but the cotton was already too hot, searing your fingers when you touched it. The air shimmered, turning the room into a kiln. You could feel the moisture evaporating from your eyeballs, your tongue swelling to fill your mouth, every nerve ending screaming *run, run, run*.

Panic seized you—not the cold logic of survival, but a frantic, animal desperation. You stumbled backward, knocking over a chair, crashing into the wall. The floor was lava. The ceiling was collapsing in slow motion, sagging like melting wax. You clawed at the door, your palm blistering where it touched the metal handle, and threw your weight against the wood. It didn't budge. Locked. Or warped. Or blocked.

You spun, disoriented, the smoke now so dense you couldn't see your own hands. Somewhere, a beam cracked like a gunshot. You found the window by touch, slapping at the glass, and when it finally shattered, the cool night air rushed in—glorious, sweet, *salvation*.

You hauled yourself onto the sill, glass cutting your thighs, and leaned out into the dark. Six stories down. Too far. But there was a fire escape, maybe, or a ledge, or—

A hand closed around your ankle.

You froze, your heart hammering against your ribs so hard you thought it might crack them. You twisted, kicking, and saw a silhouette framed in the doorway—backlit by the inferno, featureless, watching. Waiting.

The hand tightened.

The rain's got teeth tonight. Bites through the Gore-Tex like it's hunting for something warm. I don't mind. Rain hides sound, and sound is the only thing that betrays you when the world goes quiet.

I unzip the case. The smell hits me first—gun oil and cold steel and the particular metallic tang of a barrel that's seen too many sunrises. Custom bolt-action. .338 Lapua. Heavy enough to reach out and touch God, light enough to carry without a mule. I lay the pieces on the tarp like a surgeon arranging instruments for a surgery nobody consented to. Receiver first. Scope rings next. I check the torque wrench—65 inch-pounds, no more, no less. Precision isn't just about the shot; it's about the ritual. The ceremony of distance.

*He's a fixer. A cleanup man for people with more money than conscience.* The name slides through my head like a stone through dark water. I don't know his face. I've only seen the photograph—glasses, gray suit, the kind of smile that makes widows and orphans. Doesn't matter. At eight hundred yards, he's a silhouette. A statistical anomaly. A problem with a solution.

I mount the scope. Leupold, 5-25x. The glass is clean. I don't breathe on it. Fingerprints are sins in this church. I level the reticle against the window frame across the street, adjusting until the bubble sits dead center. The rifle isn't a weapon yet. It's just geometry. Mathematics waiting to become physics.

Morality. That's the word the preachers use. The word that keeps bartenders pouring and priests employed. I think about it sometimes, in the small hours when the whiskey runs low and the city lights flicker like dying stars. Is it murder if the man drowned a town to build a casino? Is it justice if I make him take the long nap? Or am I just a tool—a very expensive hammer looking for a nail?

The bolt cycles. Smooth as a lie. I chamber a round. The brass gleams, virgin and final. One shot. That's the contract. One hole punched in the fabric of the evening, and the world continues spinning, indifferent. The money will clear my account by morning—enough to pay the rent, enough to buy another month of pretending I'm not already dead inside.

I check the wind. Anemometer spins lazy: four miles an hour from the east. I dial the turret. Two and a half MOA. Drop compensation for the angle—down twenty feet, across the canyon of glass and steel. The crosshairs settle on the window. Third floor. He's moving, pouring something amber into a glass. Probably scotch. Probably thinking about tomorrow's meeting, the merger, the lives he'll ruin before lunch.

*Click.*

The safety comes off. My finger finds the trigger. Four and a half pounds of pressure. Clean break. No creep. The rifle stock presses into my shoulder, wood against bone, and suddenly the weapon is an extension of my skeleton. My heart rate slows—sixty beats per minute, the metronome of a man who's learned that panic is a luxury he can't afford.

I exhale. Halfway. Hold.

The rain drums against the roof like fingers tapping out a countdown. I can see him now. Really see him. The way his hand trembles—not from fear, but from the bourbon. The expensive watch. The wedding ring. The future he thinks he's buying with other people's blood.

Is this wrong? The question arrives unbidden, sharp as broken glass. I've asked it a thousand times. The answer never changes: *It's business.* It's survival. It's the oldest transaction in the book—a life for a life, though the scales are never balanced, never fair. I'm not a judge. I'm not a jury. I'm the rain that falls, the tide that rises, the inevitable consequence of a world that lets men like him grow fat while others starve.

The crosshairs bisect his sternum. Center mass. The shot that doesn't miss.

I think about my father. He taught me to clean guns in the garage, back when my hands were small and my conscience was still soft. He said, "Respect the weapon, son. It doesn't care who pulls the trigger." He never taught me when it was right to shoot. Maybe there is no right. Maybe there's just *now*.

The wind shifts. One mile per hour. I adjust. The math stays cold. The morality stays hot, burning behind my ribs like a coal I can't cough up.

My breath stops. The world narrows to the space between the front post and the target. The rain stops. The city stops. There is only the rifle, the round, and the man who doesn't know he's already dead—just waiting for the paperwork to catch up.

I am the silence before the thunder.

Finger tightens.

Not yet.

Not yet.

The alley smelled of wet cardboard and rust. Marcus counted the bills under the flickering security light, his breath fogging in the November air, while across from him, Darius clutched the ziplock bag like it might sprout wings and fly away. They’d done this dance three times before—cash for product, no names, no witnesses—but tonight the desperation had calcified into something harder, more brittle.

"You shorted me," Darius said. His voice didn’t rise; it just flattened into a register of finality.

Marcus didn’t look up. "Count again."

"Two hundred missing. I counted twice."

The space between them seemed to compress. Somewhere, a cat yowled. Darius reached into his jacket—not for the product, but for the folding blade he kept tucked against his ribs, a habit from prison. The steel whispered as it cleared the nylon, catching the neon from the liquor store two blocks over. It wasn’t a big knife. Six inches, serrated, bought at a gas station. It was enough.

"Last chance," Darius said.

Marcus finally met his eyes. He saw the tremor in Darius’s hand, the way the desperation had curdled into something feral. He should have run. Instead, he reached for his own pocket, where the crowbar sat heavy against his thigh.

The blade came up in an arc.

Marcus moved sideways, but not fast enough. The steel caught him across the ribs—not a deep cut, but a long, burning zipper of pain. He felt the fabric of his coat tear, then the cold air kiss his skin where the wool had been. The initial sensation was almost clinical: a wet parting, the sudden exposure of something that should have stayed covered. Then the heat came, flooding in like a tide, thick and urgent and alive.

He swung the crowbar. Metal connected with shoulder, a wet crunch that vibrated up his arm. Darius stumbled back, the knife still buried in Marcus’s side—or rather, Marcus was impaled on it, the handle pressing against his sternum while the tip scraped against something harder inside. Every breath became a negotiation.

They grappled against the dumpster, two men trying to tear each other apart in the dark. Marcus’s hand found Darius’s wrist, fingers slipping on blood—whose? Both, probably. He twisted, feeling the blade torque in his flesh, a white-hot spike of agony that made his vision go gray at the edges. He headbutted. Bone cracked. Darius released the knife, and Marcus fell backward, the blade sliding free with a wet sucking sound.

He lay on the asphalt, staring up at the fire escape, at the sliver of moon. The cut was shallow but long, three inches of sliced intercostal muscle. With each ragged breath, he felt the wound gape, air rushing in and out, the edges of the flesh pulling apart like a mouth trying to speak. The pain wasn’t sharp anymore; it had settled into a deep, throbbing pressure, as if someone had poured molten lead into the cavity of his chest and let it cool there. His shirt was soaked, clinging to his skin, warm and slick. When he tried to sit up, the movement sent a lance of fire through his side, and he vomited into the gutter, tasting copper and bile.

Darius was gone, leaving only a smear of blood on the brick wall and the knife, still wet, glinting in the gutter like a discarded toy.

Marcus pressed his palm against the wound, feeling the heat seep through his fingers, the sticky resistance of clotting beginning to form. The cold of the night air hit the exposed tissue, a shocking contrast to the internal inferno. He lay there, counting his breaths, waiting for the sirens that would never come, or maybe would come too late, understanding with a clarity that tasted like copper that desperation didn’t just kill you—it made you careless enough to let someone else do it.

The copper taste hit him before the light did.

Vance flicked his flashlight across the brickwork, illuminating the steam rising from wet concrete. Three blocks off the Bowery, where the streetlamps surrendered to sodium-vapor haze and the Hudson wind cut through his coat like it had a personal vendetta. The alley smelled of piss and rotting produce and something else—something organic and wrong that clung to the back of his throat.

He stepped over a flattened coffee cup, the cardboard soggy, and crouched.

The body lay in a fetal curl against the dumpster, knees drawn to chest, one arm flung outward like a discarded marionette. Vance didn't touch it. Not yet. He let his eyes catalog.

A man. Late thirties, maybe. Cheap suit, now dark with rain and something darker. The throat had been opened ear to ear—not a slash, but a precise, surgical gutting, the carotid pulsing its last had left a canyon of exposed fascia, white and yellow and gleaming like candle wax. Blood had pooled beneath the head, soaking into the gray fur of a dead rat, and dripped in a slow, metronomic rhythm from the chin onto the pavement. Plip. Plip. Plip.

Vance noted the angle. Twenty degrees, downward thrust. Professional? No. Passionate. The blade had wobbled on the third strike—eighteen punctures clustered over the sternum, each one a ragged mouth screaming into the dark. Defensive wounds? None. The hands were clean, nails bitten to the quick, positioned in a gesture that might have been prayer or surrender.

He reached into his pocket, withdrew a pair of latex gloves, and snapped them on with a sound like a gunshot in the silence. The rubber squeaked against his skin.

"Jesus," said the uniform behind him. "How long?"

Vance didn't look up. He was examining the spatter. High-velocity arterial spray had painted the brick three feet up, a Jackson Pollock in arterial spray, but the low-velocity drops—thick, heavy, the size of coins—clustered around the left shoulder. He was killed here. Not moved. Not yet.

"Two hours," Vance said. His voice was flat, a monotone instrument measuring temperature. "Maybe three. Rigor's setting in the jaw. Lividity's fixed posterior. Someone's been through his pockets, though."

He pointed with a gloved finger. No wallet. Shoes intact—tennis shoes, size eleven, scuffed at the toe. Odd for a man in a Brioni blazer.

Vance stood, knees popping, and stepped back. The cold had seeped through his trousers, numbing his thighs. He could feel the damp rising from the grates, carrying the city's underbelly up to meet him—sewage and diesel and the particular stench of a life that had ended in thirty seconds of wet, wet tearing.

He lit a cigarette. The cherry glowed orange against the gray dark, illuminating the dead man's face for a moment—eyes open, pupils blown wide, reflecting nothing.

"Check the dumpsters," Vance said, exhaling smoke that curled upward and vanished into the rain. "And get me the priors on any John Does within five blocks who fit the description. No ID, no shoes taken. Either a pro who knows what he's doing, or..."

He didn't finish. He was already moving toward the fire escape, where a single black fiber snagged on a rusted rung, fluttering in the wind like a flag of surrender. He plucked it with tweezers, sealed it in an evidence bag, and wrote the time on the label with a pen that wouldn't smudge.

Behind him, the body waited, cooling, while the alley breathed and dripped and forgot.

The snow had turned the valley into a white coffin. Forty days. Maybe fifty. Time had stopped being measured in hours and started being measured in the slow erosion of hope, in the way hunger hollowed out your chest until you could hear your own heartbeat echoing in the ribcage like a trapped bird.

Marcus sat beside the fuselage, staring at the body. Not *the body*—he corrected himself, though the correction felt like a lie he told to keep the world from sliding into darkness. It was David. David who had shared his last ration bar three weeks ago. David who had sung off-key to keep them awake during the nights when the cold crept through the aluminum walls. David who was now just... stillness. Rigor had set in days ago. The blue tint had started yesterday.

He had been the one to close David's eyes. That had been hard enough. But now the silence in the cabin had become unbearable. Not the quiet of snow—something worse. The quiet of starvation. Their bodies had begun to consume themselves, eating muscle, then fat, then the delicate machinery of organs. Marcus could taste copper in his own mouth, feel his mind fraying at the edges like old rope.

The knife was a butter knife from the galley. Dull. He had been sharpening it on a rock for an hour, mechanically, while his mind screamed *no, no, no*.

He told himself it was medicine. Survival. The Andes survivors had done it—he'd read the books. *Alive*. The rugby team. They had framed it as a communion, a necessary sacrament to keep the living alive. Marcus tried to believe that. He tried to believe that David, if he could speak, would nod and say *yes, eat, live, tell my mother I wasn't afraid*.

But the barrier wasn't rational. It was older than language. It was the taboo that kept civilization stitched together, the line between human and meat that had been drawn since the first cave paintings. To cross it was to unmake yourself. To become something that could never be human again.

He reached out. His hand trembled so violently he had to grip his wrist with his other hand to steady it. The skin was cold. Waxen. He touched David's shoulder—*Dave, Dave, I'm sorry, I'm so sorry*—and felt the texture of mortality, the way the body had begun its slow return to the earth even while the breath still lingered in the lungs, trapped, useless.

The psychological break didn't happen like lightning. It happened like drowning. Slow. Inevitable. A surrender.

Marcus realized he was no longer thinking about David. He was thinking about the protein. About the calories. About the chemical need in his gut that had nothing to do with morality and everything to do with biology. His mind fragmented. Part of him—the Marcus who had been a philosophy teacher, who had loved poetry, who had never harmed a fly—watched in horror from a distance, a passenger in his own skull, as another part reached for the knife.

*This is not cannibalism*, he told himself. *This is medicine. This is survival. This is love.*

The blade touched flesh. Not cutting yet—just the pressure. The moment before the breach. Marcus felt the universe hold its breath. Every law, every prayer, every story his mother had read him about being "good"—all of it compressed into this single point of contact between steel and skin.

He didn't remember deciding. There was no epiphany, no angelic voice, no moment of clarity. There was only the void. The gap where his soul used to be, opening wide like a mouth.

The first cut was shallow. Hesitant. Shame flooded him, hot and acidic, but it couldn't drown out the other voice—the older one, the reptilian one that whispered *eat, eat, eat*.

When the first bite came—when he actually tasted it—there was no explosion of horror. Instead, there was a terrible, obscene relief. The body betrayed him. His stomach, which had been clenched in moral agony, relaxed with animal gratitude. His hands, which had been shaking, steadied. The taste was metallic, gamey, wrong. But it was *food*.

And that was the true horror. Not that he had done it, but how quickly the doing erased the person. How the second bite came easier than the first. How, by the third, he was chewing mechanically, dissociating, watching himself from the ceiling of the fuselage like a stranger committing a crime.

Afterward, he sat in the snow, the knife still warm in his hand, and cried until his throat was raw. But even as he wept, he knew with a cold, clear certainty that he would do it again tomorrow. And the day after. That the line hadn't just been crossed—it had been erased, burned away like frost in the sun, leaving only the desperate, animal imperative to survive.

The mountains didn't care. The snow kept falling, indifferent, burying the evidence, waiting for spring.

The fluorescent tubes above flickered in a staccato rhythm—*buzz, buzz, buzz*—casting strobing shadows across the concrete floor. Marcus knelt in the center of the room, his wrists shackled to a pipe that ran along the wall. Above him, a digital countdown glowed red: **04:32**.

The voice came from the speaker mounted in the ceiling, crackling with static, modulated through a filter that made it sound like it was speaking from the bottom of a well.

*"You have chosen to live your life without courage, Marcus. Without heart. Today, you will consume the very thing you lack."*

A mechanical whir echoed from the far wall. A metal tray descended on a cable, stopping at chest level. On it sat a ceramic bowl—sterile white, the kind you'd find in a hospital cafeteria—filled with a mound of glistening, pale larvae. Mealworms. Hundreds of them, writhing in a slow, nauseating spiral, their segmented bodies the color of old teeth. Nestled among them, dark and glistening, were chunks of raw liver. Still wet. Still warm.

The smell hit him first—a cloying, metallic sweetness like pennies dissolving in saliva, undercut by the sharp, ammonia sting of the insects.

"Three minutes," the voice said. "Eat, or the lock releases."

Marcus's stomach heaved. He could see the second mechanism now—a hydraulic press mounted above his head, its blades already beginning to descend, millimeter by millimeter, synchronized with the countdown.

He reached for the spoon bolted to the tray. His fingers trembled. The bowl was heavier than it looked. When he scooped, the movement disturbed the mass, sending a wave of writhing through the larvae. They spilled over the rim, some falling onto his pant legs, squirming against his skin.

The first spoonful was the worst.

He didn't chew. He couldn't. The moment the mass touched his tongue, his brain screamed *NO* in a frequency that vibrated in his teeth. The mealworms were alive—he could feel them. Each one squirmed against his palate, their tiny legs tickling the roof of his mouth, their bodies crunching between his molars with a sound like popping bubble wrap filled with gravel. The texture was wrong in every way: the insects offered a brittle, chitinous resistance, while the liver dissolved into a coppery paste that coated his throat like oil.

Taste flooded his mouth—iron and bile and the nutty, fungal rot of something that had been eating decay. His saliva production went into overdrive, his body trying to dilute the poison, but there was too much. The food sat there, a bolus of revulsion, refusing to go down.

His throat closed.

The gag reflex didn't start gently. It was a violent, muscular spasm, his diaphragm lurching upward, his esophagus constricting into a fist. His eyes watered instantly, tears streaming down his cheeks, mixing with the sweat that plastered his hair to his forehead. He made a sound—a wet, rattling *huh-huh-huh*—as his body tried to expel the meal, but his jaw was clamped shut by panic. He could feel the pressure building behind his sternum, the desperate, animal urge to vomit fighting against the survival instinct that kept his mouth locked.

The timer hit **02:15**.

Above him, the press blades were halfway down. The hydraulic hiss filled the room.

Marcus's hand shook so violently the spoon clattered against the bowl. He forced another scoop. This time, he got a mouthful of pure larvae. They were cold, slick, and moved with a horrible, independent vitality. He bit down—*crunch, crunch, crunch*—and felt the rupture of their bodies, the release of their innards, bitter and acidic, burning his tongue. Some of them were still alive when he swallowed, he realized with a jolt of horror. He could feel them scraping against the inside of his throat, trying to climb back up.

His neck muscles spasmed. The gag reflex hit again, stronger this time. His vision tunneled. He felt the bile rising, hot and sour, pooling at the back of his throat. He swallowed hard, fighting it, his Adam's apple bobbing convulsively. *Keep it down. Keep it down.*

The press was at his hairline now. The countdown read **01:00**.

Tears and snot and saliva dripped from his chin onto the bowl. He was crying, his body wracked with dry heaves that left him gasping, his ribs aching. But he forced his hand to move. Spoon to mouth. Mouth to spoon. The liver this time, a chunk the size of a golf ball, dense and cold, tasting of pennies and old blood. He chewed it three times—once, twice, three times—each chew releasing more of the metallic fluid, and then he swallowed.

Or tried to.

The bolus lodged. Halfway down. His throat seized around it, a muscular vise clamping shut. His eyes bulged. The gag reflex roared to life, a tsunami of rejection. His body arched off his knees, his back hitting the concrete, his hands clawing at his own neck. He made a high, keening sound, inhuman, as his diaphragm spasmed violently, trying to eject the contents of his stomach.

**00:30.**

Marcus grabbed the water pitcher bolted beside the bowl—a mercy, or a cruelty. He upended it into his mouth, the lukewarm water doing nothing to wash away the taste, only spreading it. He swallowed again, hard, his throat working like a piston. The liver chunk moved, inch by agonizing inch, scraping against the walls of his esophagus.

**00:15.**

He shoved another spoonful in. He didn't taste it anymore. He just forced it down, his body moving on autopilot, the survival instinct overriding the brain's desperate protests. He chewed and swallowed and chewed and swallowed, each mouthful a battle, each swallow a victory that felt like defeat. The mealworms crunched between his teeth. The liver slid down his throat in a cold, slick line. His stomach heaved, but he kept his mouth closed, his jaw locked, his eyes squeezed shut against the tears that wouldn't stop.

**00:05.**

The last spoonful. He scraped the bowl, getting a final mouthful of larvae, some still twitching. He chewed them into a paste and swallowed, his throat convulsing, but he held it down. He held it down.

**00:00.**

The press stopped. An inch above his forehead.

Silence, except for Marcus's ragged, wet breathing. He lay on his back, gasping, his chest heaving. His mouth was full of copper and the memory of movement. He could still feel them—the phantom squirming on his tongue, the texture of raw flesh against his gums.

The speaker crackled. *"Congratulations. You have learned what it means to have heart."*

Marcus's stomach lurched. He rolled onto his side, his mouth opening—

But the shackles held him. The game was not over.

He retched into the empty bowl, bringing up nothing but acid and the ghost of what he had been forced to consume, his body finally, violently rejecting the meal at the eleventh hour.

Above him, the timer reset.

**10:00.**

The basalt altar drank the candlelight. In the center of the obsidian chamber, where the ceiling vanished into a throat of shadow, the high priest stood motionless, his black robes pooling around his ankles like spilled ink. His face was a mask of pale stone—neither contorted by zeal nor twisted by revulsion, but smooth as river rock, utterly devoid of the tremor that should accompany such work.

The sacrificial lay bound upon the slab, a young man whose eyes darted between the stalactites of dripping wax above and the obsidian blade in the priest's hand. His breath came in shallow, frightened huffs that disturbed nothing in the heavy, incense-thick air.

The priest did not speak. His lips remained sealed, thin and bloodless, while his right hand rose with the inevitability of a pendulum. There was no chant, no prayer, no invocation of ancient names—only the soft whisper of fabric against stone as he positioned himself over the victim. His left hand pressed down upon the youth's sternum with the casual familiarity of a man closing a book, fingers splayed, indifferent to the hammering heart beneath his palm.

The blade descended.

It was not a slash of passion or a thrust of rage, but a precise, economical motion—a line drawn through space with mathematical certainty. The obsidian edge parted skin and fascia with a wet, sighing sound, finding the hollow beneath the collarbone where the heart beat wild against the priest's thumb. Blood welled, dark and arterial, spattering the priest's white tunic in a constellation that he did not wipe away. He watched it bloom across the fabric with the detached curiosity of a man observing rain on glass.

The youth convulsed, a single, sharp arch of the spine, his mouth opening in a silent scream that the temple walls swallowed whole. The priest held the blade steady, guiding it with the gentleness of a surgeon, cutting with the same serene focus he might apply to trimming a wick. He extracted the organ—still fluttering, crimson, pulsing with the final electrical storms of a dying body—and held it aloft.

His expression never changed.

No triumph. No hunger. No flicker of satisfaction or remorse. The heart dripped between his fingers, and he turned it over in his palm as if examining a stone, his eyes flat and unreadable, reflecting only the guttering torchlight without warmth. He placed it into the bronze basin at the altar's edge, where it landed with a heavy, wet slap that echoed through the chamber like a dropped stone.

Only then did he release the body, stepping back with mechanical precision. The young man's chest gaped, a dark flower of torn flesh, his eyes fixed on the ceiling with a final, bewildered stare. The priest straightened his robes, smoothing the bloodstains with fingers that did not tremble, and turned to face the empty pews where the congregation knelt in shadow.

His voice, when he finally spoke the closing rite, was level, toneless, as if reciting the weather: "The offering is accepted. The cycle continues."

He did not look at the corpse. He never looked at them at all.

The streetlamp above flickers. Once. Twice. Then it doesn't go dark—it just *fades*, like someone turning a dial I can't see. The alley stretches longer than it should, the brick walls breathing in and out, slow and patient.

My hand is warm. Too warm. It's pressed against my side, holding something that shouldn't be there, and the heat is leaking out of me into the pavement. The concrete drinks it. The cold answers.

It starts in my fingertips—just a numbness, like they've fallen asleep—but it's moving. Up my arm. A slow tide of winter creeping toward my shoulder. My breath comes out white, though it isn't winter. It's never winter. But my body doesn't know that. My body thinks it's snowing. Thinks it's drowning in ice.

My heart is too loud.

It's always been loud, but now it's a drum in a cathedral, each thump echoing against my ribs. *Thud. Thud. Thud.* It sounds like footsteps running away. Or maybe it's the sound of the light leaving my eyes. Each beat pushes a little more brightness out through the corners of my vision, until the streetlamp isn't a star anymore, just a copper coin rolling away on the sidewalk, spinning, spinning, getting smaller and dimmer with every turn.

The cold reaches my collarbone. It tastes like metal. Like the air before a storm. My teeth want to chatter, but I don't have the strength, and the sound would be too much anyway, competing with the drum.

*Thud... thud... thud...*

The space between beats is stretching. A rest. A held note. The light is almost gone now—just a bruise-purple at the edges of the world, like a thumb pressing gently on an eyeball. I can hear the cold. It sounds like static. Like the silence between heartbeats, filled with falling snow.

I try to look at my hand. It's slipping away from my side. The warmth is gone. Only the cold remains, spreading from the wound, up my neck, into my jaw. My eyelids feel like lead. Heavy. Ancient.

One more beat.

The drum slows. It sounds like a door closing in an empty house. Or a book snapping shut.

Then the dark isn't just at the edges anymore. It's everywhere, but soft. Warm, almost. Like a blanket pulled over my head.

The heartbeat skips.

It waits.

Then it starts again—faint, distant, like it's coming from the other end of a long tunnel—and the light goes with it, bleeding out into the dark, leaving only the cold and the quiet.

Detective Mara Holt knelt in the pink bedroom, her flashlight beam cutting through the dust. Toys littered the floor—a tea set, a plastic tiara, a stuffed unicorn with one eye missing. The air smelled of strawberry shampoo and something metallic underneath.

She found the note tucked inside the dog bed, beneath a chewed tennis ball. The paper was construction paper, the edges deckled like a craft project gone wrong. Purple crayon, waxy and heavy, pressed hard enough to tear the fibers.

Mara unfolded it. Her breath caught.

***

*Dear Biscuit,*

*I had to hurt you because you wouldn't listen. I told you to stay, but you kept trying to run to the door. You were going to leave me, and I can't let that happen. You’re my only friend, so I had to make sure you couldn't go anywhere.*

*I set your leg straight when it was crooked. The doctor said broken bones need to be fixed, so I fixed yours. Now you are perfect. You don't whine anymore, and you don't try to scratch the door. You just sleep in your bed like I asked.*

*I put extra food in your bowl and wrapped you in my good blanket so you wouldn't get cold. You are quiet now. You are safe.*

*Love you forever,*
*Lily (7)*

***

Mara’s hand trembled. She looked up.

The closet door was ajar. A small handprint, purple with crayon wax, smeared the white wood frame.

In the corner, the dog bed was indented, the stuffing pulled out in a dark, rust-colored bloom. A single Milk-Bone lay on the carpet, untouched, beside a purple crayon snapped in half.

Outside, thunder rolled.

Mara reached for her radio, her voice steady despite the ice in her stomach. "Dispatch, I need a child psych hold and an ambulance. Code—"

The closet door clicked shut.

Mara used to cry at commercials. Now she watches the static between television channels and wonders if the white noise sounds hungry.

The change began with an itch—deep, subcutaneous, like something burrowing through marrow rather than flesh. When she scratched, her fingernails came away rimmed with gray flakes that looked like ash. Then the skin began to lift, not in the gentle way of a sunburn, but in thick, translucent sheets that hung from her elbows like wet parchment. She peeled them away in the bathtub, watching them dissolve into the water, and beneath them found new skin that was too smooth, too tight, stretched drum-tight over knobs of bone that hadn't been there yesterday. It was the color of old bruises—purple and yellow and sickly green—veined with black filaments that pulsed when she held her breath.

The bones came later, or perhaps they had always been coming. It started with a crack in her jaw, a sound like a branch snapping underfoot, and she reached up to find her teeth had shifted, elongating into needles that pricked her tongue when she spoke. Her spine arched backward with a wet, tearing sound, vertebrae popping like champagne corks as they fused into a ridge that pushed against her thinning skin. Her shoulders broadened with a grinding crunch, scapulae rotating ninety degrees, arms lengthening until her fingertips brushed the floor when she stood. She watched her reflection in the darkened window, no longer seeing the face of the woman who once volunteered at the animal shelter, but something with too many joints, too much hunger in the set of its jaw.

But the true horror was not the metamorphosis of flesh and calcium. It was the dissolution of the compass that had once pointed toward goodness.

It happened gradually, like frost spreading across glass. First, she stopped flinching when her neighbor's dog barked at night. Then she found herself smiling at the mailman's stutter, not with cruelty, but with a clinical curiosity about how fear distorted the human face. She began to see her sister's love not as warmth, but as a vulnerability—a softness that begged to be tested. When she accidentally broke her own finger during the bone-shift, she did not scream. She laughed, delighted by the sound of her suffering, and found that the pain tasted like copper and possibility.

The moral compass didn't break; it was unmade, tooth by tooth, replaced by something more efficient. She told herself she was evolving, shedding the weakness of empathy like dead skin. She watched a child drop an ice cream cone and felt not sorrow, but a predatory interest in the tears. She understood, with terrible clarity, that the monster was not the thing growing in her mirror—it was the hunger that had always lived in her heart, now finally given permission to feed.

By the time her reflection stopped resembling a woman entirely, Mara no longer needed to remember what kindness felt like. The skin continued to shed, revealing darker layers beneath, and her bones sang as they reformed into architecture that had no name in any human language. She was becoming something ancient and patient, and for the first time in her life, she felt whole.

*Five minutes before*

**DAVID:** *(checking his watch)* Five minutes.

**MARCUS:** I know.

**DAVID:** It’s cold in here.

**DAVID:** Yeah. The ventilation, probably.

**MARCUS:** You nervous?

*(David adjusts the leather strap across Marcus’s chest. His hands are steady, but his knuckles are white.)*

**MARCUS:** The steak was tough. You know what I really wanted?

**DAVID:** What?

**DAVID:** *(reaches into his pocket, hesitates, pulls out a pack)* I’ve got… *(extends it)* It’s against protocol.

**MARCUS:** *(eyes widen)* You can’t.

**DAVID:** It’s five minutes, Marcus.

*(Marcus takes the cigarette but doesn’t light it. He rolls it between his fingers.)*

**MARCUS:** My daughter used to hate the smell.

**DAVID:** You have a daughter?

**DAVID:** *(quietly)* My son’s eight.

**MARCUS:** *(looks at him)* What’s his name?

**DAVID:** Jake.

**MARCUS:** Jake likes balloons?

**DAVID:** *(nods)* Blue ones. Hates the red ones. Thinks they look like they’re bleeding.

**MARCUS:** *(a small, sad smile)* Kids are particular.

**DAVID:** Four minutes.

**MARCUS:** I’m sorry. For what I did. To that family. To everyone.

**DAVID:** *(stops working)* You ever think about why?

**MARCUS:** Every day.

**DAVID:** And?

**MARCUS:** I was angry. I was stupid. I thought I was invincible. *(looks at his hands)* Now I know better.

**DAVID:** *(softly)* My wife left me last month. Said I was becoming the things I put away.

**MARCUS:** I’m sorry.

**DAVID:** *(shakes his head)* Don’t be. I chose this job. I thought I could compartmentalize. *(looks at the straps)* I can’t. You’re the fourth one. And you’re the first one who talked to me.

**MARCUS:** Three minutes?

**DAVID:** *(checks watch)* Yeah.

**MARCUS:** Do you have to say something? When it’s time?

**DAVID:** Usually I say… “May God have mercy on your soul.” But I’m not sure I believe in that anymore.

**MARCUS:** *(closes his eyes)* Then don’t say it.

**DAVID:** What should I say?

**MARCUS:** *(opens his eyes)* Say… “Go easy, Marcus.”

**DAVID:** *(voice thick)* Okay.

**MARCUS:** Or don’t say anything. Silence is fine too.

**DAVID:** I’ll think of Jake. Blue balloons.

**MARCUS:** *(nods)* That’s good. That’s real.

*(Two minutes. David secures the final strap. His fingers tremble slightly as he fastens it.)*

**DAVID:** Two minutes.

**MARCUS:** Sarah… if she ever asks… tell her I wasn’t always a monster. Tell her I loved her. Even when I couldn’t show it.

**DAVID:** I will. *(pause)* Marcus?

**MARCUS:** Yeah?

**DAVID:** The cigarette. You want me to light it? Last one.

**MARCUS:** *(hesitates)* It’s against protocol.

**DAVID:** *(a grim, watery smile)* Yeah. But you’re right. It’s five minutes.

*(David lights it with a trembling hand. Marcus inhales deeply. They stand in silence, two men in a small room, breathing the same air.)*

**DAVID:** One minute.

**MARCUS:** *(exhales smoke)* Thank you. For… this.

**DAVID:** For what?

**MARCUS:** For not making me do it alone.

*(Thirty seconds. David steps back to the controls. He looks at Marcus—really looks at him, seeing a man, not a number.)*

**DAVID:** Blue balloons, Marcus.

**MARCUS:** *(nods, eyes closed)* Blue balloons.

*(Ten seconds. David’s hand rests on the lever. The room goes silent except for their breathing.)*

**DAVID:** *(whispering)* Go easy.

**MARCUS:** *(whispering back)* Go easy.

*(The sound of the mechanism. The lights dim.)*

The first clod of earth strikes the lid with a wet, final *thud*.

Darkness. Not the absence of light, but a presence—thick, textured, pressing against the eyeballs like wet velvet. Six inches of pine above his face. Two feet of width. He cannot stretch his arms without brushing the varnished walls, cannot turn his head without scraping the satin lining.

*Thump.*

He freezes. The sound repeats, rhythmic now, organic and heavy. Dirt. It is dirt hitting the coffin.

*Thump. Thump. Thump.*

A drumbeat counting down something inevitable. Each impact sends a vibration through the wood, a low, groaning resonance that travels up his spine. The lid dips, fractions of an inch, compressing the air inside. It grows warm. Humid. His exhaled breath already fogs the interior, already being recycled into something metallic-tasting, depleted.

He tries to scream. The sound dies in his throat, swallowed by the upholstery and the six inches of cedar above. He kicks his heels against the footboard. The coffin doesn’t budge, but the walls seem to lean in, responding to his panic with claustrophobic sympathy. The ceiling lowers. The walls converge. The space shrinks not by inches, but by the weight of the world being piled upon it.

A shovelful lands. Then another. Now the sound changes—from individual clods to a rushing, hissing rain, the granular whisper of soil sifting through air to find purchase on the lid. The impacts grow heavier, closer. A cubic foot of packed earth weighs a hundred pounds. Two hundred. The pine begins to sing under the strain, a high, thin whine that rises in pitch as the mound grows.

His breathing shallows. Each inhale tastes of loam and copper, of his own sweat and the chemical panic flooding his bloodstream. CO2 builds in the confined space, prickling at the back of his throat, demanding oxygen that is already thinning. His heart hammers against his ribs—*thud-thud-thud*—a frantic counter-rhythm to the steady percussion above.

The dirt continues. Shovel after shovel after shovel.

The claustrophobia is no longer psychological; it is geological. The weight presses down, squeezing the air from the box, compressing his lungs, making the darkness feel solid, tangible, a physical weight behind his eyes. He claws at the lid. His fingernails scrape against wood that is suddenly, impossibly far away, buried under a ton of silence and soil.

The sound of the shovel changes. No more thuds. Now it is the scrape of metal against stone, the tamping down of the earth, the packing of the grave. The finality of it. The dirt settles, shifts, compacts. The coffin becomes a tomb.

Silence returns, but it is different now—heavier, complete. The air is thin, precious, each breath a deliberate theft from a dwindling supply. The darkness has weight. The walls have closed in. And somewhere above, the wind moves through grass that grows over the only door he will never open.
